clips.text_zh: 我買 Zcash 賺咗 40 萬美金。youtube 同 twitter 嗰陣個個都話係 scam 嚟喎。我 2400 左右買落手，之後就同當年 BTC 咁 pump。冇人信我，嗰啲叫買賣散貨。學費又係學費，但今次係真啲。
clips.text_en_b1: I made over 400k buying Zcash. Everyone on YouTube and Twitter said it was a scam. It was pumping like old BTC before I even knew about crypto. I bought around 2400. Some people here called me a retard for buying it. Now I am down here talking about my money.
clips.text_en_b2: I made over 400k on Zcash, and the reaction on YouTube and Twitter was that the whole thing was a scam. Back then it was pumping exactly like old BTC, although I had barely even heard of crypto before that. I bought in around 2400. Some people here called me a retard for buying it. Now I'm sitting here talking about my money, and nobody believes a word of it.
clips.text_en_c1: I made over 400k buying Zcash, and at the time every single person on YouTube and Twitter was insisting it was a scam. I bought in around 2400 and watched it pump much like old BTC did, which nobody here believed. Some of the people in this thread were calling me a retard for holding it. Now I am down here talking about my money. The lesson was real, though: the tuition fee was tuition fee, but this time it was genuine, and the profits have more than paid for every mocking comment I received along the way.
clips.text_en_c2: I made over 400,000 dollars buying Zcash. At the time, practically every commentator on YouTube and Twitter insisted it was nothing more than a scam. I entered around 2,400 dollars before I had even properly understood crypto, and then it pumped in much the same way Bitcoin did in its early days. Nobody here believed me; some people responded by mocking me for buying it. Perhaps the lesson really was a lesson, although this time the money in question was genuine. Now I am down here talking about my money.
clips.source_hint: /biz/ OP says he made over 400k on Zcash bought near 2400.

clips.text_zh: MATCH Act 嘅嘢。你哋覺得佢跟住國防開支法案一齊過嘅機會大唔大？國防法案本身一定過，兩黨加埋上去，明顯就係想搞掂。而家公開反對嘅主要係荷蘭，德法喺後面。萬一過咗，ASML、ASM、SK Hynix 呢啲全部受影響lol。
clips.text_en_b1: So what do you lot think the odds are the MATCH act remains attached to the defense spending bill? The defense spending bill passing is a given. The only countries publicly and overtly lobbying against it strongly are the Netherlands, with Germany and France in the background. If it passes, ASML, ASM, SK Hynix and others are all affected.
clips.text_en_b2: So what do you lot think the odds are that the MATCH Act stays attached to the defense spending bill? The defense bill itself is going to pass, that's a given, and both parties have thrown it in there because they clearly want to get it done. The only countries openly lobbying against it hard are the Netherlands, with Germany and France lurking in the background. If it does pass, ASML, ASM, SK Hynix and everyone else in that sector are affected, lol.
clips.text_en_c1: So what do you lot make of the odds that the MATCH Act remains attached to the defence spending bill? The defence bill itself is a given, since both parties have thrown their weight behind it and it is obviously intended to go through. The only countries publicly and overtly lobbying against it are the Netherlands, with Germany and France lurking in the background. If it does pass, then ASML, ASM, SK Hynix and the rest of the semiconductor names are all affected, which is, of course, rather the point of the whole exercise.
clips.text_en_c2: What are the odds that the MATCH Act will remain attached to the defence spending bill? The defence bill itself is virtually certain to pass, and once both parties have added the chip provisions, the obvious intention is to get them enacted. The countries openly and vigorously lobbying against the measure are chiefly the Netherlands, although Germany and France are manoeuvring in the background. If it passes, ASML, ASM, SK Hynix, and several other semiconductor companies will all be affected, whether they welcome the restrictions or not.
clips.source_hint: /biz/ thread about the MATCH Act and chipmakers like ASML and SK Hynix.

clips.text_zh: IT'S ABSOLUTELY OVER。中國 AI 嘅進步完全停咗。現有嘅 LLM 開始出事，因為 anthropic poisoning。中國人根本冇創新，最強嘅 refining 俾 AI 取代晒。你用平嘅 AI 當 worker agent 都唔夠用，好多人話佢花幾個鐘喺 Claude instructions 度，乜都冇。所以不如直接用 Claude。廢柴連呢啲都唔識用。
clips.text_en_b1: IT'S ABSOLUTELY OVER. Progress in Chinese AI has completely stalled. Existing LLMs are beginning to experience problems due to Anthropic poisoning. Many users reported that these cheap AIs spend hours on Claude instructions with no results, so it is better to just use Claude directly.
clips.text_en_b2: IT'S ABSOLUTELY OVER. Progress on Chinese AI has stalled completely, and existing LLMs are starting to break down because of Anthropic poisoning. Chinese developers simply aren't innovating anymore, since the strongest refining work has been taken over by AI itself. Plenty of people report that these cheap models waste hours on Claude instructions and get nowhere, so you're better off just using Claude directly. Idiots don't even understand that much.
clips.text_en_c1: IT'S ABSOLUTELY OVER. Progress in Chinese AI has completely stalled. Existing LLMs are beginning to break down because of Anthropic poisoning. Chinese developers have, frankly, shown little appetite for genuine innovation, and the strongest refining work has simply been replaced by AI. Even if you try to deploy the cheap models as worker agents, they are not good enough; plenty of people have reported that they spend hours buried in Claude instructions and accomplish absolutely nothing. So why bother, when you can just use Claude directly? Idiots cannot even figure out how to do that properly.
clips.text_en_c2: IT'S ABSOLUTELY OVER. Progress in Chinese artificial intelligence has come to a complete standstill, and existing large language models are already beginning to falter because of Anthropic poisoning. China has produced virtually no genuine innovation; even the strongest model-refinement work has been displaced by AI. If you are using a cheap AI as a worker agent, it may not be adequate for the job. Numerous users have reported that these models spend hours struggling with Claude instructions and accomplish nothing whatsoever. Why not simply use Claude directly? Idiots evidently cannot even grasp that option.
clips.source_hint: /g/ thread claiming Chinese AI development has stalled and cheap models are unusable.

clips.text_zh: 世界歷史上最大事件仲有 9 日。12 月 5 號有兩棲入侵 Kharg Island，一艘美國航母會被擊沉。之後美軍會用核武回應打伊朗。跟住第二日 12 月 6 號星期日，俄羅斯同中國會一齊攻擊美國，俄羅斯仲會打西歐。如果你仲有你條命就準備啦。
clips.text_en_b1: BIGGEST EVENT IN WORLD HISTORY HAPPENS IN 9 DAYS. On the 5th of December there will be an amphibious invasion of Kharg Island, and a US carrier will be sunk. A nuke will then be used on Iran by the USA. On the 6th, Russia and China will attack the United States.
clips.text_en_b2: THE BIGGEST EVENT IN WORLD HISTORY HAPPENS IN 9 DAYS. On December 5th there will be an amphibious invasion of Kharg Island, and a US carrier will be sunk. After that, the Americans will answer Iran with a nuclear weapon. Then on the following day, December 6th, which is a Sunday, Russia and China will attack the United States together, and Russia will also hit Western Europe. If you've still got your life, you'd better get ready.
clips.text_en_c1: THE BIGGEST EVENT IN WORLD HISTORY HAPPENS IN NINE DAYS. On the 5th of December there will be an amphibious invasion of Kharg Island, and a US carrier will be sunk. The United States will then respond with a nuclear strike on Iran. On the following day, the 6th, which falls on a Sunday, Russia and China will attack America simultaneously, with Russia also going after Western Europe. If you still have your life, then you had better start preparing, because this particular timeline leaves no room for anyone who is caught sitting still.
clips.text_en_c2: THE BIGGEST EVENT IN WORLD HISTORY WILL HAPPEN IN NINE DAYS. On 5 December, an amphibious invasion will strike Kharg Island, and an American aircraft carrier will be sunk. The United States will then respond to Iran with nuclear weapons. The following day, 6 December, which is a Sunday, Russia and China will launch a joint attack against the United States, with Russia also turning its attention towards Western Europe. If you still have your life, then it is time to prepare.
clips.source_hint: /pol/ thread predicting a Gulf invasion and a US-Russia-China war on December 5-6.

clips.text_zh: 我做咗 Starting Strength 三個星期。squat 70 x 5 x 3，deadlift 82.5 x 5，bench 40 x 5 x 3，press 22.5 x 5 x 3。我知 press 係弱jb，但第一兩次連空槓都掂唔穩。想問，我幾時應該減慢 squat 加 5 公斤同 deadlift 加 7.5 公斤嘅速度？我未試過 fail work set，係咪應該一直加到 fail 為止？
clips.text_en_b1: I'm doing SS since 3 weeks. Squat 70 x 5 x 3 kilos, deadlift 82.5 x 5, bench press 40 x 5 x 3, press 22.5 x 5 x 3. My question is: when should I slow down on the 5 kilos jump on the squat and the 7.5 kilos jump on the deadlift? Should I continue until I fail?
clips.text_en_b2: I've been running Starting Strength for three weeks now. Squat 70 x 5 x 3 kilos, deadlift 82.5 x 5, bench press 40 x 5 x 3, and overhead press 22.5 x 5 x 3. I know the press is embarrassingly weak, since I could barely hold the empty bar steady on my first couple of sessions. My question is: when should I slow down the 5 kilo jump on the squat and the 7.5 kilo jump on the deadlift? I've never failed a working…
clips.text_en_c1: I have been running Starting Strength for three weeks now. Squat 70 x 5 x 3, deadlift 82.5 x 5, bench press 40 x 5 x 3 and press 22.5 x 5 x 3. I know that my overhead press is pathetically weak, and for the first couple of sessions I could not even stabilise the empty bar. My question, therefore, is when I should start slowing down the five-kilo jump on the squat and the seven-and-a-half-kilo jump on the deadlift. I have never actually failed a working set, so should I simply keep adding weight until I do, or is there a more sensible trigger for backing off?
clips.text_en_c2: I have been following Starting Strength for three weeks. My squat is 70 kilograms for five repetitions across three sets, my deadlift 82.5 kilograms for five, my bench press 40 kilograms for five across three sets, and my overhead press 22.5 kilograms for five across three. I know the press is pathetically weak, but during my first couple of sessions I could barely control even an empty bar. When should I reduce the rate at which I add five kilograms to the squat and 7.5 kilograms to the deadlift? Since I have never failed a working set, should I simply keep increasing the weight until I do?
clips.source_hint: /fit/ OP asks when to slow down Starting Strength weight jumps.

clips.text_zh: Pixiv Fanbox 拎走 Paypal 同 Mastercard 信用卡呢個選項。RIP 晒嗰啲想獨立、唔想俾 dumb editors 管嘅 mangaka。我諗香港畫師都一樣受影響，donate 呢家野遲早要行多過一條 payment channel。靠，收唔到錢就當用 AI 續命。
clips.text_en_b1: Pixiv Fanbox is removing the Paypal and Mastercard credit card payment option. RIP to those mangaka who want to be independent from dumb editors. The linked Fanbox posts confirm the change. A lot of indie artists are now looking for other ways to take payments.
clips.text_en_b2: Pixiv Fanbox is dropping the Paypal and Mastercard credit card option entirely. RIP to all those mangaka who wanted to stay independent and refuse to be managed by dumb editors. I bet Hong Kong artists are hit by the same thing, and donations are always going to need one more payment channel eventually. Fine, if the money doesn't come in, I'll just keep myself alive with AI art.
clips.text_en_c1: Pixiv Fanbox is dropping the Paypal and Mastercard credit card payment option, which has been confirmed by the linked Fanbox posts. RIP to all those mangaka who wanted to be independent and refuse to have dumb editors running their lives. I suspect Hong Kong artists are affected in exactly the same way. Everyone who relies on donations will eventually need another payment channel, and at some point there is simply no way around it. If the money cannot be collected, then so be it; the plan becomes using AI to keep the whole thing alive for a few more months.
clips.text_en_c2: Pixiv Fanbox has eliminated the PayPal and Mastercard credit-card payment option. Rip to those mangaka who wanted independence from incompetent editors and resented being micromanaged. The linked Fanbox posts confirm that this change is indeed happening. Hong Kong artists are likely to be affected in the same way, since donating money through such platforms has inevitably required an increasing number of payment channels. Fine; if the money cannot be collected, the survivors can simply use artificial intelligence to keep themselves alive.
clips.source_hint: /a/ thread about Pixiv Fanbox removing Paypal and Mastercard payments.

clips.text_zh: Borderlands。支線任務做晒係因為 perfectionism 啦，而支線先係 RPG 嘅重點。但去到第五條主線就已經 overpowered，成個敵人低過你十幾級，個 game 再都冇難度可言。我求其個隻支線 grind 完算係，睇完算。
clips.text_en_b1: Borderlands. Do every side quest out of perfectionism, and also it is the whole point of RPGs. By the 5th main quest you are way overpowered and every enemy is multiple levels below you. The game is never hard again. So does it still matter?
clips.text_en_b2: Borderlands. I do every single side quest because I'm a perfectionist, and honestly the side quests are the whole point of an RPG. The problem is that by the fifth main quest you're already overpowered, and every enemy ends up more than ten levels below you. At that point the game has no difficulty left in it whatsoever. So I might as well grind through the side content, watch it all, and call it done.
clips.text_en_c1: Borderlands. I completed every single side quest out of sheer perfectionism, and side quests are arguably the whole point of an RPG rather than a side distraction. By the time I reached the fifth main quest I was hopelessly overpowered, with every enemy sitting multiple levels below me, and the game simply never felt difficult again. So does any of this still matter? I am just going to grind through the remaining side content for the sake of it and consider the game finished once I have seen the credits.
clips.text_en_c2: Borderlands. I complete every side quest out of sheer perfectionism, and side quests are, after all, the central pleasure of an RPG. Yet by the fifth main mission, the player is hopelessly overpowered: every enemy is more than ten levels beneath you, and the game loses any meaningful sense of difficulty. There is no point in struggling with the combat once that imbalance takes hold. I may as well grind through the remaining side quests, watch them conclude, and call it a day.
clips.source_hint: /v/ thread about doing every Borderlands side quest and enemy scaling.

clips.text_zh: 我買 Zcash 蝕咗 20萬美金。YouTube 同 Twitter 個個都話係 THE PLAY！我 1200 左右入嘅，唔知點解就係唔郁。此刻我哋叫你交學費就得，唔使驚，贏嘅時候我靜靜地收。呢個唔係金融規劃，係賭命。
clips.text_en_b1: I lost over 200k buying Zcash. Everyone on YouTube and Twitter said it was the play! It was pumping like old BTC before I even knew about crypto. I bought around 1200 and it just kept bleeding. Anyway, tuition. Same again tomorrow.
clips.text_en_b2: I lost over $200,000 buying Zcash after people on YouTube and Twitter repeatedly insisted it was “the play.” Although it was pumping like old Bitcoin before I even knew much about crypto, I bought in at around $1,200, and it kept bleeding. At this point, paying tuition seems reasonable: collect it later and enjoy the profits quietly. This is not financial planning; it is gambling with my life.
clips.text_en_c1: I lost over $200,000 buying Zcash. Everyone on YouTube and Twitter insisted it was “THE PLAY,” and it was pumping like old BTC before I even knew what crypto was. I bought in at around $1,200, and the price simply kept bleeding. Looking back, I should have realised that the confidence surrounding the asset was completely disconnected from its performance. This was not financial planning; it was gambling with my money. Anyway, tuition paid. The same again tomorrow.
clips.text_en_c2: I lost over $200,000 buying Zcash. Everyone on YouTube and Twitter insisted it was THE play, and the token was pumping like old Bitcoin before I had even properly understood crypto. I entered at around $1,200, yet the price simply kept bleeding, day after day, while the crowd remained conspicuously confident. The prevailing wisdom was reassuring: pay the tuition, do not panic, and quietly bank the profits when the move finally arrives. In hindsight, this was not financial planning; it was gambling with borrowed certainty. The painful part is that every piece of advice I followed came from people who had already seen the pattern elsewhere.
clips.source_hint: /biz/ anon confesses a 200k loss on Zcash after buying near 1200.

clips.text_zh: 假設你拎咗 30萬美金出嚟，唔限時間揀你想買乜，但有個條件：4 個月後要還返晒 30萬，唔還就俾黑幫用刑，仲要 torture 到死。利潤全部歸你，賺剩多少都係你嘅。我會 half put 去 bond，half 溝 gold，唔好孭住。成本回報先算清楚。
clips.text_en_b1: Imagine you get 300k to invest into anything you like, whenever you like, but there is only one condition. You must return all of the 300k after 4 months, or you get vanned by mafia and tortured to death. You keep 100% of the profits. What would you do?
clips.text_en_b2: Imagine receiving $300,000 to invest in anything you wanted, whenever you wanted, with only one condition attached. You would have to repay the entire $300,000 after four months; otherwise, the mafia would have you “vanished” and tortured to death. In return, you would keep every cent of the profit. Although the returns sound extraordinary, I would split the money between bonds and gold rather than hold everything, because calculating the cost and potential return comes first.
clips.text_en_c1: Imagine you are handed $300,000 to invest in whatever you want, whenever you want, with only one condition: after four months, you must return the entire $300,000. If you fail to repay it, the mafia will take you and torture you to death. You keep 100% of whatever profits you make, with no limit on how long you can trade. What would you do? I would put half into bonds and half into gold, and I would not carry the entire position. If the expected return does not clearly justify the risk, then even the potential profit is irrelevant.
clips.text_en_c2: Imagine that you are handed $300,000 to invest in absolutely anything you choose, whenever you choose, with one non-negotiable condition: four months later, you must repay the entire $300,000. Fail, and the mafia will collect the debt by torturing you to death. The incentive is unusually severe, since you retain 100 percent of whatever profits you generate; losses, naturally, remain your problem. If it were me, I would place half in government bonds and half in gold rather than keep the entire sum in cash. The first task would be to calculate the expected return against the risk-adjusted cost of repayment.
clips.source_hint: /biz/ hypothetical thread: 300k to trade, must return it in 4 months or die.

clips.text_zh: Fidelity 遲咗先至 apply 緊 spot Chainlink ETF，仲要隔日先開 direct LINK trading。S-1 都入咗 SEC。呢個唔同 institution partnership 嗰種要等幾年，spot ETF 係直接嘅 demand。Chainlink 講真係 infra，我成日喺度睇 oracle 啲嘢。
clips.text_en_b1: Major LINK-positive development: on November 25, 2026, Fidelity filed an S-1 registration statement with the SEC for the Fidelity Chainlink Fund. This comes just one day after Fidelity introduced direct LINK trading to its customers. A spot ETF can translate into token demand much faster than institutional partnerships.
clips.text_en_b2: There is a major development for LINK, because Fidelity has filed an S-1 registration statement with the SEC for the Fidelity Chainlink Fund. This came just one day after the company introduced direct LINK trading for its customers. Unlike an institutional partnership, which can take years to develop, a spot ETF may create direct demand much more quickly. Chainlink also has serious underlying infrastructure behind it; I frequently follow the oracle space and believe that strength is worth paying attention to.
clips.text_en_c1: A major LINK-positive development has emerged: on November 25, 2026, Fidelity filed an S-1 registration statement with the SEC for the Fidelity Chainlink Fund. The filing came just one day after Fidelity introduced direct LINK trading for its customers. Unlike institutional partnerships, which may take years to develop and produce results, a spot ETF could translate into demand for the underlying token much faster. Chainlink is, in my view, genuine infrastructure rather than merely another speculative asset, particularly because I regularly follow developments in oracle technology and its role in the broader ecosystem.
clips.text_en_c2: A major positive development for Chainlink has emerged: on November 25, 2026, Fidelity filed an S-1 registration statement with the SEC for the Fidelity Chainlink Fund. The timing is especially notable because Fidelity introduced direct LINK trading for customers just one day earlier. Unlike an institutional partnership, which may take years to produce meaningful adoption, a spot ETF can translate investment demand into token demand much more directly. There is also a straightforward technological argument for LINK’s relevance. Chainlink provides essential infrastructure for oracle services, and I frequently examine the way those systems operate. This filing may not guarantee sustained inflows, but it represents a considerably more immediate route to market exposure.
clips.source_hint: /biz/ thread says Fidelity filed for a spot Chainlink ETF after adding direct LINK trading.

clips.text_zh: IT'S ABSOLUTELY OVER。Progress in Chinese AI 已經完全停咗。現有 LLM 開始有問題，因為 anthropic poisoning。你哋啲細 AI 用做 worker agent 越來越廢，幾個鐘都做唔完 Claude 嘅 instructions。所以最好直接用 Claude。靠AI續命，AI都係咁。
clips.text_en_b1: IT'S ABSOLUTELY OVER. Progress in Chinese AI has completely stalled. Existing LLMs are beginning to experience problems due to Anthropic poisoning. Many users report that these cheap AIs spend hours on Claude instructions with no results, so it's better to just use Claude directly.
clips.text_en_b2: IT’S ABSOLUTELY OVER. Progress in Chinese AI has completely stalled, although existing LLMs are already showing problems because of Anthropic poisoning. Many users report that cheap AI models spend hours struggling with Claude instructions and never produce a usable result. Although these smaller models are increasingly used as worker agents, their declining performance makes them almost useless for serious tasks. It would be better to use Claude directly, because trying to extend the life of weaker AI just prolongs the same problem.
clips.text_en_c1: IT’S ABSOLUTELY OVER. Progress in Chinese AI has completely stalled, and existing large language models are beginning to encounter serious problems because of Anthropic poisoning. Many users claim that cheaper AI systems can spend hours struggling to complete Claude’s instructions without producing a meaningful result. If those models are increasingly unreliable when used as worker agents, there is little reason to use them instead of paying for Claude directly. Relying on AI to extend our lives and solve problems does not change the underlying equation; the weaker systems still remain weak, regardless of how convenient they are.
clips.text_en_c2: IT’S ABSOLUTELY OVER. Progress in Chinese AI has completely stalled, while existing large language models are beginning to show problems attributed to what the poster calls Anthropic poisoning. The practical complaint is that cheaper Chinese models, when assigned as worker agents, frequently spend hours attempting to follow Claude’s instructions without producing anything useful. If that is the prevailing experience, why not use Claude directly and spare yourself the wasted time? Relying on AI to keep ordinary work moving is hardly an improvement when the cheaper alternatives remain so unreliable. The pattern is depressingly familiar: artificial intelligence is supposed to extend our capabilities, yet here it merely extends the delay.
clips.source_hint: /g/ thread claims Chinese AI progress stalled and cheap models are unusable as agents.

clips.text_zh: 呢個 board 點解成日有人跪舔中國？佢哋係殘忍嘅非人，虐待動物，尤其係貓，最慘酷嗰種。根本冇 animal cruelty law，Chinese social media 充滿虐待內容。仲要有人話「咁你又唔講 jews running America」，噏。香港都一樣，貓狗冇保障。
clips.text_en_b1: Why is there so much Chinese dicksucking on here? They're cruel inhuman freaks that torture animals, especially cats, in the most horrific ways they can. There are no animal cruelty laws in China, and Chinese social media is filled with abuse content. Anyone who replies with 'why don't you talk about the Jews running America' is a chink shill deflecting.
clips.text_en_b2: Why does this board contain so many people who defend China at every turn? They are cruel and inhumane, abusing animals, especially cats, in the most horrific ways imaginable. Although China has no proper animal-cruelty law, its social media is full of abuse material. Anyone who responds with “why don’t you talk about the Jews running America” is merely deflecting, and the hypocrisy is staggering. Hong Kong is no better, because cats and dogs have virtually no legal protection there either.
clips.text_en_c1: Why is there so much pro-Chinese worship on this board? The people involved are cruel and dehumanising, particularly when they torture animals, especially cats, in the most horrific ways imaginable. There is effectively no meaningful animal-cruelty law in China, and Chinese social media is filled with disturbing abuse content. Anyone who replies with “Why don’t you talk about the Jews running America?” is merely deflecting the issue rather than answering it. Hong Kong is no different in this respect: cats and dogs still have virtually no legal protection from abuse.
clips.text_en_c2: Why does this board contain so much apologetic praise for China? The people being defended are, according to the original poster, cruel and inhuman beings who torture animals, especially cats, in the most horrific ways imaginable. China has no meaningful animal-cruelty law, and Chinese social media is allegedly saturated with disturbing abuse material. Even worse, some defenders evade the issue by asking why nobody discusses “the Jews running America,” which does nothing except redirect attention away from the alleged mistreatment. Hong Kong is no better: cats and dogs there likewise have little legal protection. The point is not that criticism becomes less objectionable because its target belongs to a particular ethnicity; it is that cruelty should be condemned on its own terms.
clips.source_hint: /pol/ thread about Chinese animal cruelty and deflection in debates.

clips.text_zh: 74 kg 體重，180 kg 死舉 x5。每次都係一 set of 5 或者更多。Home floor press 36 kg kettlebells，每組至少 15 下，加 band pull aparts 每 2 日 gym 一死舉。肥仔信成日話我唔好淨係掛住死舉，wtf。
clips.text_en_b1: My method of bodybuilding: at home floor press with 36 kg kettlebells for at least 15 reps each day, each set followed by band pullaparts. Every 2 days at the gym, a deadlift set of 5 or more reps. 180 kg x 5 at 73 kg bodyweight. Also stop bumping my threads, why are they still up?
clips.text_en_b2: My bodybuilding method is straightforward: at home, I floor-press with 36-kilogram kettlebells for at least 15 repetitions, followed by band pull-aparts. Every two days, I visit the gym and complete a set of five or more deadlift reps, reaching 180 kilograms at a bodyweight of 73 to 74 kilograms. Although some online “fitness experts” keep telling me not to focus exclusively on deadlifting, they are wrong. Meanwhile, people are still bumping my threads, so why have they not been removed yet?
clips.text_en_c1: My approach to bodybuilding is unconventional. At home, I floor press with 36-kilogram kettlebells for at least 15 repetitions every day, completing each set with band pull-aparts. Every second day, I go to the gym and perform a deadlift set of five or more repetitions. The latest result was 180 kilograms for five reps at a bodyweight of 74 kilograms, or 73 kilograms according to the earlier post. People who are out of shape keep telling me not to focus exclusively on deadlifting, which is rather ironic, since they seem to have little interest in making any progress themselves. Also, why are my old threads still up?
clips.text_en_c2: My method of bodybuilding is deliberately unglamorous. At home, I floor-press with 36-kilogram kettlebells, completing at least 15 repetitions every day, with each set followed by band pull-aparts. Every second day, I go to the gym and perform a deadlift set of five or more repetitions; the best result is 180 kilograms for five reps at a bodyweight of roughly 73 to 74 kilograms. Apparently, the standard advice is that I should not rely exclusively on deadlifts, which is a remarkably unimaginative response to a training programme that includes press work and accessory work. The original poster also asks people to stop bumping his threads and wonders why they remain up; clearly, even elite lifting strength has not solved the problem of obsessive online disputation.
clips.source_hint: /fit/ poster logs a 200 kg x3 deadlift at 74 kg bodyweight and complains about thread bumping.

clips.text_zh: Do you think Steins;Gate has left a legacy on the anime industry? It's one of those anime that feels like it's in between classic status and your normal popular show。我睇完第二季仲係覺得神，但隔籬有啲神作真係神。Gundam 00 同埋呢套，都係同一個年代。
clips.text_en_b1: Do you think Steins;Gate has left a legacy on the anime industry? It's one of those anime that feels like it's in between classic status and your normal popular show. Some fans say it changed how sci-fi time travel stories are told, others just call it a classic.
clips.text_en_b2: Do you think Steins;Gate has left a lasting legacy on the anime industry? It occupies an unusual space between the canonical classics and ordinary popular entertainment. Although I still found the second season genuinely brilliant after finishing it, some nearby masterpieces are even stronger; Gundam 00, for example, came from the same era. Some fans argue that Steins;Gate changed the way science-fiction stories handle time travel, whereas others simply regard it as a classic, and both reactions capture why it still matters.
clips.text_en_c1: Do you think Steins;Gate has left a lasting legacy on the anime industry? It occupies an unusual position between a fully established classic and an ordinary popular show, yet its influence is difficult to dismiss. Even after finishing the second season, I still consider it exceptional, although several works from the same period are arguably even stronger. Gundam 00, for example, belongs to roughly the same era and demonstrates just how demanding the standard can be. Some fans argue that Steins;Gate changed the way science-fiction time-travel stories are structured and presented, while others simply regard it as a classic.
clips.text_en_c2: Do you think Steins;Gate has left a lasting legacy on the anime industry? It occupies an unusual position: neither an ordinary mainstream favourite nor a universally acknowledged classic, yet arguably more substantial than both categories suggest. After finishing its second season, I still regarded it as extraordinary, although several neighbouring works from the same period—among them Gundam 00—were, in my view, even more remarkable. Some fans maintain that Steins;Gate reshaped the way science-fiction stories handle time travel, whereas others simply classify it as a classic. That divided reaction may actually be the clearest evidence of its influence: its ideas have become embedded in the genre’s vocabulary, even when the consensus about its status remains unsettled.
clips.source_hint: /a/ thread asking whether Steins;Gate counts as a classic or just a popular show.

clips.text_en_c2: GTA 6 recompilation thread. Our boy Claude has unquestionably come a long way. At this rate, perhaps within five years AI systems will conduct site investigations themselves, leaving the rest of us to sit around, eat peanuts, and watch. For now, the footage remains startling rather than fully conclusive: impressive as it is, one successful recompilation does not yet amount to a general-purpose replacement for skilled software engineering.

clips.text_en_c1: I lost over 200k buying Zcash, and I regret every single satoshi of it. Back in the day it was pumping like early Bitcoin was, and I trusted every hype thread on YouTube and Twitter without doing my own research. I bought roughly 1,200 units, which sounded like nothing until the price collapsed. Damn it, another round of very expensive tuition. These days I can barely summon the energy to cry; I just stare at the chart and question my life choices, wondering whether I learned anything at all or simply handed my savings to people who were laughing at me.
clips.text_en_c2: Another tuition fee, this time paid in crypto. Zcash had been pumping as if it were the next Bitcoin, so, naturally, I trusted every glowing assessment on YouTube and Twitter and bought roughly 1,200 units. The result speaks for itself: a loss of more than 200k. Watching the chart now is enough to make me question my judgment, although I am too drained even to cry. I suppose the lesson is painfully familiar: if an asset is promoted as an obvious winner by people who have nothing to lose, it may be precisely the moment to ask whether the consensus has left room for disappointment.
clips.source_hint: A /biz/ trader recounts losing more than $200,000 after buying Zcash near 1,200.

clips.text_zh: 如果畀你300k，4個月後要還返本金，賺到嘅全部own，蝕本就要俾 mafia「處理」。最安全係short-term bonds，甚至放savings account。咁都有人高風險all-in，膠膠吶，我可能先學識保住本金。
clips.text_en_b1: Imagine you get 300k to invest whenever you like. You must return all 300k after four months, or face death by the mafia. You keep every profit. Short-term bonds or savings would be safest, but the risk-reward is still brutal.
clips.text_en_b2: Imagine being given 300k to invest whenever you like. After four months, you must return the full 300k, while all the profits are yours to keep; fail, and the mafia will ‘deal with’ you. Short-term bonds or a savings account would be the safest options, although the risk-reward remains brutal. Some people would still go all-in with high-risk bets, but perhaps I need to learn how to protect my principal first.
clips.text_en_c1: Imagine someone hands you 300k to invest, whenever you feel like it. Whatever you make, you keep; but after four months you must return the entire principal, and if you fail to do so, the mafia will handle you. Short-term bonds, or simply parking it in a savings account, would be the safest route, and yet some people still go all-in on high-risk plays, which is idiotic. The risk-reward ratio remains brutal either way. If I were in that position, I suspect I would finally learn what it actually means to protect a principal sum rather than chase spectacular returns.
clips.text_en_c2: Suppose someone gave you 300k to invest for precisely four months, with no strings attached until the deadline. You would have to return the entire principal, while every penny of profit belonged to you; failing to repay the money would invite the mafia to collect it by whatever means they considered appropriate. Under those conditions, the sensible options would be short-term bonds or, failing that, a savings account. Even so, some people would probably go all-in on something volatile, because greed has a remarkable talent for disguising recklessness as conviction. Personally, I suspect the real lesson is to preserve the capital first; otherwise, no amount of theoretical profit is worth being liquidated.
clips.source_hint: A risk puzzle asks what to do with $300,000 under a four-month repayment condition.

clips.text_zh: Optimus已經係god-tier carpenter，組裝速度快到離譜。靠AI續命啦，咁快連hardware都識做？工程上最怕個workflow突然由人變robot，仲要成個load path都要重新驗。
clips.text_en_b1: Literally how is this even possible? Optimus is already a god-tier carpenter. It assembles things at an insane speed. How?? This makes me wonder whether engineering workflows will soon be checked by robots too.
clips.text_en_b2: How is this even possible? Optimus already seems like a god-tier carpenter, assembling things at an absolutely insane speed. Apparently, AI is keeping it going, but how quickly robots are learning to make hardware is unsettling. From an engineering perspective, the scary part is that the workflow could suddenly shift from human workers to robots, meaning the entire load path would have to be reassessed and verified.
clips.text_en_c1: Literally, how is this even possible? Optimus is already a god-tier carpenter: the assembly speed is absurd, and the footage is genuinely difficult to square with what robotics could realistically achieve today. If AI is the thing keeping it alive, then how long before the hardware itself can be manufactured by robots? What genuinely worries me from an engineering standpoint is that a workflow which has always relied on human judgement could abruptly be replaced by automated review, and every load path would need to be revalidated from scratch. That transition would not be an incremental upgrade; it would be a wholesale rethink.
clips.text_en_c2: How on earth is this possible? Optimus already looks like a god-tier carpenter, assembling components at a frankly absurd speed, and the sight of AI keeping the operation alive raises an unsettling question: how long before hardware itself becomes autonomous? The deeper issue, however, is engineering rather than spectacle. Once part of the workflow shifts from human hands to robotic systems, every tolerance, process, and safety assumption must be reassessed. Even the load path cannot simply be inherited unchanged; it has to be revalidated from first principles. If those checks pass, the result may be transformative. If they do not, speed will have achieved little more than manufacturing mistakes more efficiently.
clips.source_hint: A /g/ thread praises Optimus for its extremely fast assembly work.

clips.text_zh: 點解咁多年輕人被powerlifting呃？有人只係想fit啲、靚啲，結果被叫住bulk，body fat一路升，barbell training仲未必最optimal。考牌已經夠stress，唔想連body image都交學費。
clips.text_en_b1: How did so many young men get tricked into powerlifting? Most guys just wanted to get in shape and look decent. Instead, they are told to bulk up, gain fat, and use barbell training that may not be optimal for their goals.
clips.text_en_b2: How did so many young men get tricked into powerlifting? Most simply wanted to get in shape and look decent, yet they end up being told to bulk up, gain body fat, and follow barbell training that may not be optimal for their goals. The competition tests are stressful enough on their own; I certainly don’t want to pay additional tuition with my body image as well.
clips.text_en_c1: How did so many young men end up getting tricked into powerlifting? Most of them simply wanted to get fitter, look better in a shirt, and feel healthier; instead, they are told to bulk, watch body fat climb steadily, and adopt barbell programming that may not be remotely optimal for their actual goals. The programming itself is questionable for plenty of beginners. Add the stress of preparing for a meet and the psychological pressure of being judged on a platform, and you have a recipe for a serious body-image problem.
clips.text_en_c2: How did so many young men end up being lured into powerlifting when their original ambition was merely to become fitter and look better? The answer lies in a culture that treats the barbell as the unquestionable gateway to an impressive physique, even though gaining body fat is not identical to becoming healthier. Bulking is often presented as obligatory, yet the prescribed approach may do little to serve an individual’s actual goals. On top of that, preparing for a competition is stressful enough without surrendering control of one’s body image to somebody else’s rigid methodology. There is no shame in wanting to look decent. There is, however, a lesson to be learned before paying tuition fees with your health and self-confidence.
clips.source_hint: A /fit/ thread argues that many beginners adopt powerlifting and bulking unnecessarily.

clips.text_en_b1: Do you think Steins;Gate has left a legacy on the anime industry? It is one of those anime that feels between classic status and your normal popular show. Its story and ideas still feel solid years later.
clips.text_en_b2: Do you think Steins;Gate has left a lasting legacy on the anime industry? Although it never became as mainstream as many popular shows, it seems to occupy a strange place between classic status and ordinary mainstream anime. Its story and ideas still feel solid even years later, and some works that you revisit a decade later somehow retain a powerful sense of world-building and emotional depth.
clips.text_en_c1: Do you think Steins;Gate has genuinely left a legacy on the anime industry? It is one of those shows that occupies an uneasy space between unquestioned classic status and the sort of mainstream fare most people actually consume. It never became the biggest name in the room, which is precisely why it tends to age well. Its story, its ideas, and the emotional texture of its world still feel remarkably solid a decade on, and there are works I have revisited years later that have lost none of their weight. That kind of staying power is rarer than it looks.
clips.text_en_c2: Has Steins;Gate left a genuine legacy on the anime industry? I believe it has, although its status never quite fitted the categories that mainstream fandom tends to create. It is neither an obscure cult production nor merely one more popular anime destined for a brief surge of nostalgia; instead, it occupies an uneasy middle ground between canonical classic and ordinary mainstream entertainment. That position is arguably more revealing. A work that can be rediscovered a decade later and still feel structurally sound, emotionally coherent, and intellectually relevant has achieved something rarer than immediate popularity. Its world-building and ideas continue to withstand the passage of time, suggesting that its influence rests on lasting substance rather than nostalgia alone.
clips.source_hint: An /a/ thread discusses Steins;Gate and its place in anime history.

clips.text_en_c1: I spent years absorbing the nonsense billionaires tend to produce once they have accumulated enough wealth to disregard the consequences. clips.text_en_c2: I spent years internalising the sort of provocative nonsense billionaires unleash once they have accumulated enough wealth to treat public opinion as optional. In reality, ordinary observers rarely get within shouting distance of these figures while they are still making money, which makes their pronouncements particularly revealing. clips.text_zh: Elon又出嚟講智能嘅秘密。靠AI續命就靠AI續命啦，但真係work就最緊要。Civil engineering個工都可能俾AI逐步取代，靠AI續命。
clips.text_en_b1: Elon just spilled secrets about what makes something intelligent. The post suggests that understanding intelligence could affect future AI development. For engineers, the useful question is where AI will replace technical work first.
clips.text_en_b2: Elon has once again spoken publicly about the secrets of intelligence, apparently revealing more about how it works. Although AI can keep the market alive, what matters most is whether it actually works in practice. Understanding intelligence could shape the next stage of AI development, particularly in technical fields. For engineers, the practical question is which parts of civil engineering will be replaced first, and whether AI will take on routine technical work before it handles more complex responsibilities.
clips.text_en_c1: Elon has once again offered his thoughts on the elusive nature of intelligence, claiming to have revealed some of its underlying secrets. Given that AI is currently carrying much of the market’s optimism, whether his explanation actually works is more important than the publicity surrounding it. The wider implication is that understanding intelligence could shape the next phase of AI development, particularly as increasingly capable systems are introduced into professional settings. For engineers, the practical question is which parts of technical work will be automated first. Civil engineering is a plausible target, although some roles may be augmented rather than replaced outright.
clips.text_en_c2: Elon has once again offered tantalising hints about what actually constitutes intelligence, although the broader implications remain less certain than his confident presentation suggests. If understanding intelligence can shape the next phase of AI research, it may also transform how engineers approach cognitive tasks, interfaces and automation. The genuinely useful question is not whether AI will eventually replace civil engineering, but where it will displace specialised technical work first. Routine analysis, drafting and routine design may already be under pressure, whereas complex judgement and accountability remain more resilient. AI may keep the profession alive, but only if engineers adapt rather than simply compete with the technology.
clips.source_hint: A short tech post says Elon revealed ideas about intelligence.

clips.text_zh: 點解歐洲政府連jet bridge都買唔起？香港成個地方咁逼，完全唔夠位。連基本基建都搞唔掂，講咩其他。wtf。
clips.text_en_b1: Why can’t European governments afford jet bridges at airports? The question highlights the strange gap between airport passenger capacity and the infrastructure available to serve those passengers. It is also a practical example of transport investment problems.
clips.text_en_b2: Why can’t European governments even afford jet bridges at their airports? The issue exposes a strange gap between the number of passengers an airport can handle and the infrastructure available to serve them once they arrive. Although basic facilities may appear straightforward to provide, planning, construction, and maintenance are far more complicated. Hong Kong, by comparison, is extremely crowded and seems to lack sufficient space. If governments cannot manage essential airport infrastructure, it is difficult to take their wider transport commitments seriously.
clips.text_en_c1: It is difficult to understand why European governments, which can finance large-scale transport projects, appear unable to provide basic jet bridges at many airports. The issue exposes an awkward gap between nominal passenger capacity and the infrastructure needed to serve those passengers efficiently. Hong Kong offers an even more familiar example of extreme crowding, where passengers are routinely accommodated in genuinely cramped conditions. Neither example necessarily proves that governments are wholly incapable of investing in aviation; the underlying causes could involve cost, procurement, planning, and competing priorities. Nevertheless, if essential airport infrastructure remains inadequate, ambitions for greater capacity sound hollow.
clips.text_en_c2: Why can’t European governments apparently afford jet bridges at some of their airports? The question exposes a peculiar mismatch between passenger capacity and the physical infrastructure required to serve it. A terminal may be modernised, security may be automated and boarding may proceed through sophisticated digital systems, yet passengers can still be funnelled through a limited number of gates and corridors, forcing congestion, delays and improvised boarding arrangements. Hong Kong offers an even starker illustration of what happens when available space cannot accommodate demand. This is not an isolated procurement failure so much as a broader failure of transport planning, in which visible infrastructure is treated as an afterthought. If the essentials are not managed competently, grander ambitions are difficult to defend.
clips.source_hint: The thread asks why some European governments cannot afford airport jet bridges.

clips.text_en_c1: A reminder to all AI toddlers: train a model on GPL-licensed code, then exploit that as a loophole to have it generate the very same code back. Everyone who uses current AI models to write code may, in effect, be participating in licence laundering, since the underlying training material was never freely licensed for such reuse. Your talent for phrasing a request politely and clicking "generate" does not make you the author of the output, and the original author may very well retain the rights to it. clips.text_en_c2: A reminder to all self-proclaimed AI toddlers: one can train a model on GPL-licensed code and then exploit the resulting system as a loophole to reproduce code of the same kind. The ability to formulate a polished request, click “generate,” and paste the result does not make a person the author of the output; intellectual property does not transfer merely because a machine produced the text. The original author may still own the relevant rights, so checking the licence remains indispensable.

clips.text_en_c1: The low-bar squat is genuinely one of the worst exercises ever popularized. Rather than delivering meaningful quad stimulation, it mostly fries the central nervous system and turns the movement into a posterior-dominant hip-and-glute hinge as soon as the bar drops even slightly lower. Depth is usually rubbish, yet some fat powerlifters defend the variation because they can move more weight by effectively turning a squat into a good morning. If the load path shifts toward the hips and glutes, then simply sinking lower does not automatically make the exercise better. clips.text_en_c2: The low-bar squat is genuinely one of the worst exercises ever to have been popularised. For most lifters, it wrecks the central nervous system while doing little to develop the quadriceps, the muscle group it is conventionally assumed to train. Lower the bar even slightly and the movement becomes a posterior-dominant hinge: the hips and glutes take over, the torso folds forward, and the quads receive comparatively little stimulation. Depth is usually rubbish as well, since the range of motion ends once the lifter can no longer preserve a sensible spinal position. Fat powerlifters tend to defend the exercise because they can move heavier loads by converting a squat into a good morning with a barbell, but added weight is not synonymous with a better exercise.
clips.source_hint: The OP argues that low bar squats use a bad movement pattern and train quads poorly.

clips.text_en_b1: WHY IS EVERYTHING DOWN? Gold, stocks, crypto, oil, and bonds are all falling. These are the big five assets. Normally, when one market falls, another should rise. But tonight, all five are down at the same time. It feels like every CFD position is bleeding.
clips.text_en_b2: Why is the entire market behaving so ridiculously? Gold, stocks, crypto, oil and bonds—the big five asset classes—are all falling together. Normally, when one market drops, another should pick up the slack, but tonight every CFD position seems to be bleeding. At this rate, I will be paying prop firm tuition soon and relying on AI to keep the account alive.
clips.text_en_c1: Why is the entire market behaving so irrationally? Gold, stocks, crypto, oil, and bonds—the big five asset classes—are all falling at once. Ordinarily, if one market weakens, another should offer refuge, but tonight every CFD position appears to be bleeding. Even the usual retail logic that diversification should provide protection has collapsed. At this rate, a prop firm tuition bill may be harder to stomach than the losses. Either someone is deliberately dismantling the market, or investors have suddenly realised that these supposedly unrelated assets were never independent in the first place.
clips.text_en_c2: Why is the entire market behaving as though it has collectively lost its mind? Gold, equities, cryptocurrency, crude oil, and government bonds—the big five asset classes—are falling in unison. In the textbook world, strength in one market should offset weakness elsewhere, yet tonight every CFD position seems to be bleeding at once. It is the kind of synchronised rout that makes retail investors start hunting for some hidden rotation or contrarian trade. If this persists, the joke about prop-firm tuition becomes uncomfortably realistic, with artificial intelligence presumably helping us survive long enough to pay it.
clips.source_hint: A /biz/ poster asks why all five major asset classes are falling together.

clips.text_zh: 有人話Grok一直trailing，所以Musk先sell compute畀競爭對手，俾佢哋reverse engineer同偷偷研究模型。Neuralink、SpaceX都照搞，唔知條tech line仲可唔可信。Musk stock要小心，唔係淨係講笑。
clips.text_en_b1: Possibility: Grok is failing, and so is Musk. Grok may be trailing or failing, while Musk sells compute to competitors. They can reverse engineer the software and infer the inner workings of his models. If that is true, Tesla and SpaceX investors need to examine the risk.
clips.text_en_b2: One possibility is that Grok is failing badly, although that does not necessarily mean Musk is failing with it. If Grok is trailing its rivals, Musk may be selling compute to competitors, allowing them to reverse engineer the software and infer how the models work internally. Neuralink, SpaceX and Tesla are still proceeding, but investors should seriously examine the risk rather than dismiss it as a joke.
clips.text_en_c1: One possibility is that Grok is underperforming badly and Musk is consequently selling computing capacity to competitors. Once they obtain the software, they can reverse engineer it, infer how the models work, and quietly investigate their weaknesses. If that interpretation is correct, it raises uncomfortable questions for anyone who has treated Neuralink, SpaceX, or Tesla as part of one credible technology empire. Investors should examine the risk rather than dismiss the issue as routine business criticism. Musk’s stock may be particularly vulnerable if technical leadership cannot be independently verified.
clips.text_en_c2: One possibility is that Grok is faltering and, by extension, so is Musk. If Grok is trailing its rivals or failing outright, Musk may be selling access to scarce computing capacity to competitors, enabling them to reverse-engineer the software and infer the inner workings of his models. That would be more than an embarrassingly technical problem; it would raise serious questions about the defensibility of his wider technological strategy. Neuralink and SpaceX may continue apace, but investors should no longer assume that every venture in his portfolio rests on equally solid engineering. Tesla and SpaceX shareholders ought to examine that risk rather than dismiss it.
clips.source_hint: A /biz/ post argues that Grok's failure and Musk's compute sales may be connected.

clips.text_zh: 隔籬有人問可唔可以將斜坡安全交畀AI。靠，靠AI續命可以，factor of safety就唔可以亂靠。GI report要睇 soil condition、groundwater同 load path，drainage同 soil nailing都要一齊 check。
clips.text_en_b1: Engineering judgment still matters on every slope. GI reports need real soil data, groundwater information, and the correct load path. Drainage, soil nailing, and factor of safety must also be checked. AI can help organize the data, but it cannot replace engineering judgment.
clips.text_en_b2: Can slope safety really be left to AI? Sure, AI might keep the report alive, but the factor of safety cannot be delegated carelessly. A proper geotechnical investigation requires reliable information about soil conditions, groundwater and the load path. Drainage, soil nailing and the final factor of safety must also be checked. AI can organise the data, yet it cannot replace sound engineering judgment.
clips.text_en_c1: Slope safety cannot be delegated to AI, although AI may be useful for organising the relevant information. Every engineering assessment still requires sound judgment, particularly when deciding whether a factor of safety is appropriate. The geotechnical investigation report must establish real soil conditions, groundwater levels, and the load path through the slope. Drainage provisions, soil nailing, and the overall factor of safety also need to be checked rather than inferred from generic assumptions. If the supporting data are incomplete or unreliable, no algorithm can manufacture a defensible conclusion; it can only make an unsupported recommendation sound deceptively authoritative.
clips.text_en_c2: No, engineering judgment still matters on every slope, even if artificial intelligence is willing to lend a hand. A geotechnical investigation report must be grounded in reliable soil data, clearly established groundwater conditions, and a correct understanding of the load path. Drainage, soil nailing, reinforcement, and the appropriate factor of safety cannot simply be delegated to a model and then treated with unearned confidence. AI can usefully organise observations, compare scenarios, flag inconsistencies, and accelerate preliminary calculations; it cannot substitute for professional judgment, site-specific assessment, or accountability when the consequences of an error are potentially catastrophic.
clips.source_hint: A /g/ user asks which technical path to take while working remotely.

clips.text_zh: 第一次去紐約住一個月，想體驗下day-to-day life。ChatGPT叫佢去Astoria，anomo又建議Upper East Side。香港咁迫住都冇乜所謂，去到美國反而要計安全同人種，wtf。
clips.text_en_b1: NYC. I'll be staying in NYC for a little over a month, and it will be my first time there. Where is a good, safe place to experience day-to-day life? ChatGPT told me to stay in Astoria. But what about the Upper East Side? Please advise.
clips.text_en_b2: NYC. I will be staying in the city for a little over a month, and it will be my first time experiencing day-to-day life there. ChatGPT recommended Astoria, while Anomo suggested the Upper East Side. Could someone advise on a good, safe place to stay? In Hong Kong, crowding is a problem, but in America I now have to calculate safety and demographics as well.
clips.text_en_c1: I’m going to New York for a little over a month, and it will be my first time there, so I would like advice on where to stay safely while experiencing ordinary day-to-day life. ChatGPT suggested Astoria, while anomo recommended the Upper East Side. The latter may offer a more central base, although safety and the demographic mix are both factors I have never had to consider in Hong Kong, where most people simply tolerate crowded living conditions. It feels absurd that someone accustomed to such density should suddenly be calculating these risks in America. Any firsthand recommendations would be welcome.
clips.text_en_c2: I am heading to New York for a little over a month, and it will be my first time there, so I would like to experience ordinary day-to-day life rather than merely tick off the usual tourist sights. ChatGPT has recommended Astoria, while anomo has suggested the Upper East Side. I would be grateful for advice on which neighbourhood offers a good combination of convenience, safety, and an authentic feel. The contrast is striking: crowding is accepted as a fact of life in Hong Kong, whereas in the United States one apparently has to consider safety and racial demographics before choosing where to live. Any recommendations from people who know the city would be welcome.
clips.source_hint: A /pol/ visitor asks where to stay during his first month in New York City.

clips.text_zh: 以前係lardass，想lean bulk真係好難。以前成日busy到冇時間track macros，只係食多啲protein同健康少少嘅嘢。但最驚又fat返，lifts又冇進步。肥仔信今日又叫我入gym，Damn。
clips.text_en_b1: Hi /fit, former lardass here. Can I get a body-fat estimate and some tips for slowly bulking without getting too fat? I struggle to progress with lifting because I am busy and all over the place. I do not track macros, but I try to eat a high-protein, mostly healthy diet.
clips.text_en_b2: Hi /fit, former lardass here. Could I get an estimate of my body fat and some advice on bulking up without gaining too much fat? I used to be quite chubby, and lean bulking sounds difficult. Because I am always busy, I never tracked macros; I simply tried to eat more protein and otherwise healthier food. My biggest fear is getting fat again without improving my lifts. The gym called me back today, damn.
clips.text_en_c1: Hi /fit, former lardass here, and I would appreciate a rough body-fat estimate alongside some advice on starting a lean bulk. In the past, I tended to eat whatever was available and gradually gained more fat than muscle, which makes deliberate bulking genuinely difficult. I am usually too busy to track macros consistently, although I do try to eat a high-protein, mostly healthy diet and train regularly. My main concern is that, if I increase my intake, I will become fat again without making any meaningful progress in the lifts. Could a former lardass get away with doing little more than eating and hitting the gym?
clips.text_en_c2: Hi /fit, former lardass here, and I would like to put my finances where my mouth is by trying a slow lean bulk. Unfortunately, that transition is far more difficult than simply eating a little more, particularly when my training, work, and schedule leave little room for meticulous tracking. I do not currently count macros, although I try to maintain a high-protein diet based mostly on healthier foods. My main concern is that a surplus of calories will simply translate into renewed fat gain while my lifts stagnate, which would make the whole endeavour rather pointless. I am finally being dragged back to the gym, so any practical advice would be extremely welcome.
clips.source_hint: A former overweight lifter asks for body-fat advice and a lean-bulk plan.

clips.text_en_b1: New GPUs, including Intel Xe, AMD RX 7000 and 9000 series, and NVIDIA RTX 40 and 50 series, now work in Windows 7 with an unofficial WDDM 2 backport. DirectX 12 also works. The poster says there is no real reason to use Windows 10 or 11 anymore.
clips.text_en_b2: New graphics cards, including Intel Xe, AMD RX 7000 and 9000 series, and NVIDIA RTX 40 and 50 series, can now run on Windows 7 through an unofficial WDDM 2 backport. DirectX 12 works as well. According to the poster, there is therefore no real reason to use Windows 10 or 11. As AI continues to consume GPUs, even older cards may become more valuable, lol.
clips.text_en_c1: New GPUs, including Intel Xe cards, AMD’s RX 7000 and 9000 series, and NVIDIA’s RTX 40 and 50 series, can now operate in Windows 7 through an unofficial WDDM 2 backport. DirectX 12 also works, according to the poster, who concludes that there is no compelling reason to remain on Windows 10 or 11. That is a striking development for anyone willing to run an unsupported system, especially since continued AI demand may gradually increase the value of older graphics hardware. The workaround may not be suitable for ordinary users, but it certainly gives vintage PCs a new lease of life.
clips.text_en_c2: Modern graphics cards are now usable in Windows 7 after all. An unofficial WDDM 2 backport enables support for Intel Xe, AMD RX 7000 and 9000 series, and NVIDIA RTX 40 and 50 series hardware, with DirectX 12 also functioning. The poster’s conclusion is blunt: there is ostensibly no compelling reason to prefer Windows 10 or 11, particularly for users who value the continuity of an older system. There is also a broader commercial implication, since artificial intelligence continues to absorb cutting-edge GPU capacity and may drive up demand for otherwise obsolete cards. Whether that will make old hardware more valuable remains uncertain, but the thought is certainly amusing.
clips.source_hint: A /g/ post describes an unofficial Windows 7 driver backport for modern GPUs.

clips.text_en_b2: Since the Iran war began, Bitcoin has outperformed both gold and silver, continuing to outperform precious metals during a broader market collapse. The poster argues that BTC is now the asset worth holding when confidence in traditional safe havens is fading, although no entry price or stop-loss level is provided. The view is strongly bullish on Bitcoin, but it comes with a warning: although AI may keep the market alive for a while, traders should avoid adding excessive leverage and should hold their positions carefully.
clips.text_en_c1: BTC has once again outperformed both gold and silver. Since the Iran war began, it has consistently outpaced precious metals while the broader market has been collapsing. clips.text_en_c2: Since the Iran war began, Bitcoin has decisively outperformed both gold and silver, maintaining its advantage throughout the resulting market turmoil. The poster argues that if a genuine collapse is imminent, BTC is the asset most worth holding, although the conviction comes without a stated entry price or stop-loss level. What the post does not provide is a coherent risk-management framework, so the impressive relative performance should not be mistaken for a complete investment strategy.

clips.text_en_b1: Miners are getting rekt. Copper, uranium, gold and silver, and lithium are all dumping like shitcoins. The poster asks whether this is a buying opportunity or whether people should keep waiting. No specific trade or price level is provided.
clips.text_en_b2: Miners are getting rekt again, with copper, uranium, gold and silver, and lithium all dumping like shitcoins. Although such a sharp decline can look like an opportunity to buy a dip, the poster is clearly unsure whether prices have reached a genuine bottom or whether investors should continue waiting for a better setup. clips.text_en_c1: Miners have been comprehensively rekt once again. Copper, uranium, gold and silver, along with lithium, are all plunging as though they were worthless shitcoins rather than valuable commodities. The poster is genuinely uncertain about what this prolonged sell-off represents: is it a buying opportunity for those willing to catch a falling knife, or should investors continue waiting for conditions to improve? Although the question suggests someone who understands the sector, no specific trade, entry price, or price target is offered, leaving the analysis at the level of market sentiment rather than a concrete plan.
clips.text_en_c2: Miners are being comprehensively rekt as copper, uranium, gold and silver, and lithium all tumble like failed shitcoins. The sharp sell-off leaves prospective investors with an uncomfortable dilemma: treat the correction as a buying opportunity, or remain sidelined until the underlying trend becomes clearer? The poster offers no particular trade, asset, or price level, nor does he claim that the decline has fundamentally altered these commodities. What is evident is widespread carnage across several mining-linked sectors at once. Whether that breadth signals an unusually attractive entry point or the early stage of a longer downturn remains unresolved, making the decision less about timing than conviction in the eventual recovery.
clips.source_hint: A /biz/ thread asks whether the metals and mining sell-off is a buying opportunity.

clips.text_zh: Nvidia 話builder攞唔到GPU，搞到manufacturing scarcity。有人話Jensen淨係識將GPU賣俾自己啲人，gameers同builders就係活該。AI bot同shill反而唔理。靠AI續命，連磚都冇得砌，wtf。
clips.text_en_b1: Nvidia is denying GPUs to builders, creating manufacturing scarcity. The post blames Jensen Huang and says AI bots and paid shills ignore what is happening to gamers and builders. It also mentions alleged illegal shipments to China and artificial scarcity.
clips.text_en_b2: Nvidia is denying builders access to GPUs, creating severe manufacturing scarcity in the process. The post blames Jensen Huang for allegedly selling GPUs to people close to the company while ignoring the difficulties faced by gamers and builders. It also refers to illegal shipments to China and artificial scarcity, arguing that AI bots and paid shills remain indifferent to the damage. The result is a shortage serious enough that even people trying to build physical systems cannot obtain the hardware they need.
clips.text_en_c1: Nvidia is allegedly restricting builders’ access to GPUs, thereby creating severe manufacturing scarcity. The poster blames Jensen Huang, arguing that he merely sells hardware to people who are already close to him while ordinary gamers and independent builders are left with nothing. AI bots and paid shillers, meanwhile, are said to ignore the damage. The post also refers to shipments to China allegedly violating US export restrictions and to artificial scarcity designed to inflate prices. Frustrated by the idea that AI is keeping the industry alive, the poster complains that even building bricks may become impossible.
clips.text_en_c2: Nvidia is restricting builders’ access to GPUs, manufacturing an artificial scarcity that is obstructing production rather than serving ordinary users. The post directs much of its criticism at Jensen Huang, portraying him as someone who merely sells GPUs to favoured insiders while gamers and builders are left to fend for themselves. AI bots and paid shills, according to the writer, conveniently ignore the damage. The thread also alleges illegal shipments to China, a further claim that compounds Nvidia’s supposed disregard for the law. The underlying frustration is that advanced hardware, ostensibly driven by innovation, is becoming less available precisely to the people expected to build with it, leaving scarcity as an extractive business model.
clips.source_hint: A /g/ thread discusses Nvidia GPU shortages, Jensen Huang, and alleged illegal shipments to China.

clips.topic_en: AI and the Future of Jobs
clips.text_zh: 如果Elon講嘅嘢係真，兩年內可能冇晒工作。剩低嘅只係做billionaire同AI agent嘅menial labor。香港咁細，連廢物都冇位擺，唔知AI會唔會連civil engineering都ko咗。
clips.text_en_b1: If what Elon says is true, there may be no more jobs in two years. Only menial labor for billionaires and their AI agents would remain. The post asks what will happen to ordinary workers if this future becomes real.
clips.text_en_b2: If Elon Musk’s claims are accurate, there may be virtually no jobs left within two years. The only roles that remain would be menial labour performed for billionaires and their AI agents, while ordinary workers would face unemployment on a massive scale. The post also raises a more immediate question about Hong Kong, a city so tightly packed that even waste disposal is difficult: what happens to civil engineering and other practical sectors if AI begins replacing them too?
clips.text_en_c1: If Elon Musk’s predictions are taken at face value, there may be virtually no employment left within two years. The only work remaining would be menial labour performed by billionaires’ AI agents, with ordinary employees largely excluded from the economy. The poster is especially sceptical about Hong Kong, a city already so densely developed that even waste disposal presents a spatial problem. They then widen the concern to civil engineering: if AI can replace skilled professional work as well as routine jobs, what role, if any, remains for people who have spent years acquiring specialised expertise?
clips.text_en_c2: If Elon Musk’s prediction proves accurate, employment could disappear within two years, leaving humanity with little more than menial labour performed for billionaires by their AI agents. That prospect is already enough to provoke alarm, particularly in Hong Kong, where space is so scarce that even waste must find somewhere to go; if AI eliminates routine work, what remains for ordinary people whose practical knowledge encompasses civil engineering? The post does not examine the assumptions behind Musk’s forecast, but it captures the anxiety shared by workers who suspect that technological progress may benefit capital owners far more readily than the people it displaces.
clips.source_hint: A /pol/ thread asks about mass job loss, billionaires, and AI agents.

Cutting feels easier because gaining weight scares me, although my lifts have not really progressed. Despite remaining disciplined enough to cut, however, my lifts have not improved for some time, suggesting that the approach may need to be more carefully structured.
clips.text_en_c2: A former lardass checking in with the /fit community, seeking an estimate of current body-fat percentage and advice on how to begin a slow bulk without simply reaccumulating fat. He describes a demanding work schedule that leaves little room for meticulous macro tracking, although his diet is consistently high in protein and otherwise reasonably balanced. The psychological obstacle appears greater than the nutritional one: cutting has paradoxically felt easier because regaining weight frightens him, while his lifting performance has stagnated despite sustained effort. Any sensible response would therefore need to acknowledge both his history of overeating and his limited capacity for obsessive measurement, rather than prescribing an elaborate protocol he may never follow.
clips.source_hint: A /fit/ thread asks about body-fat estimation and lean bulking after gaining weight.

clips.text_en_b1: Are anime memes still happening? The poster remembers 2000s manga tropes, doujin pages, and panels becoming recognizable internet icons. They mention the new Cyberpunk: Edgerunners season and its chromed-up memes, but say few newer anime memes travel beyond their own series.
clips.text_en_b2: Are anime memes still happening? After watching a Yu-Gi-Oh storytime, I began missing the distinctive tropes of 2000s manga, doujin pages, and panel images that became instantly recognizable across the internet. Although the new season of Cyberpunk: Edgerunners has produced some “chromed up” reactions, apparently very few newer anime memes have managed to escape their own series and become widely shared cultural references. The nostalgic post suggests that anime-related humour may now live mainly within dedicated fandoms rather than circulating freely online.
clips.text_en_c1: Does anybody still remember when anime memes genuinely circulated online? After watching a Yu-Gi-Oh storytime, the poster began nostalgic for 2000s manga tropes, doujin pages, and individual panels that became instantly recognisable internet icons. Although Cyberpunk: Edgerunners has recently returned for another season and inspired the familiar “chromed up” format, the broader anime community apparently struggles to produce memes that escape their originating series. The implication is that anime humour has become increasingly insular: jokes may briefly exist within a fandom, yet they rarely achieve the wider cultural reach enjoyed by earlier meme eras.
clips.text_en_c2: The poster wonders whether anime memes still exist in any meaningful cultural sense, since watching a Yu-Gi-Oh storytime revived nostalgic memories of 2000s manga tropes, doujin pages, and individual panels transformed into recognisable internet icons. Those older examples escaped their original fandoms and became shared language across the wider web. By contrast, although Cyberpunk: Edgerunners has a new season and produces the inevitable “chromed up” jokes, most of its memes apparently remain confined to the series itself. The lament is not simply that anime has stopped generating memorable images, but that contemporary fandom seems increasingly insular: jokes circulate intensely among existing fans without acquiring the broader, self-sustaining life that once made them portable cultural artefacts.
clips.source_hint: An /a/ thread asks whether anime memes still move beyond their original series.

clips.text_zh: 大家開始信CEO嘅hype，轉頭又quote CEO，仲要當佢哋係自己公司嘅推廣員。Musk講過就當confirm，Nvidia嗰位chinky man講過亦一樣。咁點解唔信個sell used cars嘅人？
clips.text_en_b1: People trust CEOs because they repeat whatever the CEOs say. They quote company leaders as if every statement is proof, while trusting used-car salesmen far less. The post says these are basically the same behavior, then asks whether people are simply retarded.
clips.text_en_b2: People are increasingly accepting a CEO’s hype, repeating it as evidence and then quoting the same executive as if he were the official promotional voice of the entire company. If statements from Musk are treated as confirmation, why should anyone treat Nvidia’s leadership differently? The post draws a deliberately provocative comparison with used-car salesmen, who are generally viewed as unreliable when making claims. Its central question is whether audiences are simply being gullible, although it expresses that criticism in an offensive way.
clips.text_en_c1: People have started treating corporate CEOs as authoritative sources, then promptly quoting them as though every statement constituted independent proof. Musk’s remarks are treated as confirmation simply because he made them, and the same unquestioning attitude is extended to Nvidia’s CEO, whom the poster disparagingly refers to as a “chinky man.” Yet if accepting self-promotional claims from powerful technology executives is reasonable, why is the used-car salesman regarded with such suspicion? The poster highlights the inconsistency: when the message comes from a celebrated CEO, the audience appears willing to abandon basic scepticism and become free publicity for the company.
clips.text_en_c2: The post highlights an apparent contradiction in how investors treat corporate authority: audiences accept a CEO’s every utterance, quote it approvingly, and then deploy it as evidence while conveniently ignoring its promotional provenance. Musk’s remarks are treated as confirmation, and the same credulous acceptance extends to Nvidia’s famously blunt chief executive; why, the writer asks, should a used-car salesman not command similar faith? The underlying criticism is that celebrity, media visibility, and market position are mistaken for independent verification. A confident delivery does not make a forecast truthful, nor does repeating a claim make it more reliable. The irony lies in investors demanding extraordinary scepticism from ordinary salespeople while surrendering it entirely to powerful figures whose incentives are rarely neutral.
clips.source_hint: A /biz/ post mocks investors for trusting CEO hype, including Musk and Nvidia leadership.

clips.text_en_c1: AI is now openly decoding ciphers. In a post dated 16 November, DeepMind prompt engineer fofr reported that a model had located Giovanni Bianco's 1465 key in a Vienna index after 71 decoding runs. The process began with scans for which no transcript existed; the model transcribed handwritten cipher signs, applied statistical solvers, and then searched European archives. What was once painstakingly manual detective work is becoming an automated pipeline. Even archaeology can apparently be delegated to AI, which is reassuring for scholars and rather less so for those whose expertise depends on being marginally slower.
clips.text_en_c2: AI is now openly decoding ciphers. In a post dated 16 November, DeepMind prompt engineer fofr reported that a model located Bianco’s 1465 key within a Vienna index after 71 decoding runs. The process began with scans that lacked any transcript; from there, the system transcribed handwritten cipher signs, applied statistical solvers, and searched European archives for Giovanni Bianco’s key. What was once the preserve of patient human scholars is becoming an automated pipeline, which is reassuring for archaeology, provided one remains employable. AI for longevity, apparently, though career prospects look considerably less certain.
clips.source_hint: The post describes an AI system decoding a handwritten historical cipher after repeated attempts.

Sometimes a person is not simply lazy or deficient in effort; sometimes the world is simply unjust, and no amount of individual grit will make the odds stack in your favour.
